instruments.title: Technology Risk Management Guidelines — consultation draft (P003-2019)

mandates.title: Apply never-alone, segregation of duties and least privilege
Run an approved process to provision and revoke access
Log user access activity under unique identities
Enforce a strong password policy
Use multi-factor authentication for critical functions
Review user access periodically
Grant access only on a need-to-use basis and revoke promptly
Restrict and monitor service providers like staff
Limit, log and review privileged access
Monitor system and service accounts
Encrypt remote access and require strong authentication
Allow remote access only from hardened devices
Perform regular vulnerability assessments
Cover minimum scope in vulnerability assessments
Conduct black-box and grey-box penetration tests
Consider a bug bounty programme to complement testing
Penetration-test production with proper safeguards
Set penetration test frequency by risk and exposure
Run scenario-based cyber exercises and review plans
Involve stakeholders in cyber exercises
Consider adversarial attack simulation exercises
Define rules of engagement for red-team exercises
Base red-team scenarios on real cyber incidents
Alternatively design scenarios from threat intelligence
Track and resolve assessment findings by severity
Safeguard the development and provision of APIs
Control access to designated API services
Vet third parties before granting API access
Assess risk before third parties connect via APIs
Set secure API standards and protect keys and tokens
Encrypt sensitive data sent through APIs
Test APIs before production and log third-party sessions
Monitor APIs in real time and revoke keys on breach
Handle high API volumes and mitigate denial of service
Govern third-party and open-source code before use
Track vulnerabilities in third-party and open-source code

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.1
evidence.text: The principles of ‘never alone’, ‘segregation of duties’, and ‘least privilege’ should be applied when granting staff access to information assets so that no one person has access to perform critical system functions. Access rights and system privileges should be granted according to the staff’s role and job responsibilities.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.2
evidence.text: The FI should establish a user access management process to provision and revoke access rights to information assets. Access rights should be authorised and approved by the information asset owner.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.3
evidence.text: For accountability, the FI should ensure records of user access and user management activities are uniquely identified and logged for audit and investigation purposes.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.4
evidence.text: The FI should establish a password policy and a process to enforce strong password controls for users’ access to IT systems.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.5
evidence.text: Multi-factor authentication should be implemented for users with access to critical system functions to safeguard the systems and information from unauthorised access.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.6
evidence.text: The FI should ensure information asset owners perform periodic user access review to verify the appropriateness of privileges that are granted to users. The user access review should be used to identify dormant and redundant user accounts, as well as incorrectly provisioned access rights. Exceptions noted from the user access review should be resolved as soon as practicable.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.7
evidence.text: The FI should ensure users are granted system access rights on a need-to-use basis. Existing access rights that are no longer needed, as a result of a change in a user’s job responsibilities or employment status (e.g. transfer or termination of employment), should be revoked or disabled promptly.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.1.8
evidence.text: The FI should subject its service providers, who are given access to the FI’s information assets, to the same monitoring and access restrictions on the FI’s personnel.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.2.1
evidence.text: Users granted with privileged system access have the ability to inflict severe damage on the stability and security of the FI’s IT environment. Access to privileged accounts should only be granted on a need-to-use basis; activities of these accounts should be logged and reviewed as part of the FI’s ongoing monitoring.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.2.2
evidence.text: System and service accounts are used by the operating systems, applications and databases to interact or access other systems’ resources. The FI should establish a process to manage and monitor the use of system and service accounts for suspicious or unauthorised activities.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.3.1
evidence.text: Remote access allows users to connect to the FI’s internal network via an external network to access the FI’s data and systems, such as emails and business applications. Remote connection should be encrypted to prevent data leakage through network sniffing and eavesdropping. Strong authentication, such as multi-factor authentication, should be implemented for users performing remote access to safeguard against unauthorised access to the FI’s IT environment.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 9.3.2
evidence.text: The FI should ensure remote access to the FI’s information assets is only allowed from devices that have been hardened according to the FI’s security standards.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.1.1
evidence.text: The FI should establish a process to conduct regular vulnerability assessment (VA) on their systems to identify security vulnerabilities and ensure risk arising from these gaps are addressed in a timely manner. The frequency of VA should be commensurate with the criticality of the system and the security risk to which it is exposed.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.1.2
evidence.text: When performing system VA, the scope should minimally include vulnerability discovery, identification of weak security configurations, as well as applications and services that are not approved by business, IT management and other key stakeholders. For web-based systems, the scope of VA should include checks on common web-based vulnerabilities, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.2.1
evidence.text: The FI should carry out penetration testing (PT) to obtain an in-depth evaluation of its cyber security defences. A combination of blackbox and greybox testing should be conducted for online financial services.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.2.2
evidence.text: A bug bounty programme is another mean by which an FI could discover vulnerabilities in their systems by inviting and incentivising ethical or “white hat” hackers to test their systems. The FI may consider conducting a bug bounty programme to test the security of its IT infrastructure to complement its PT.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.2.3
evidence.text: To obtain a more accurate assessment of the robustness of the FI’s security measures, PT should be conducted on the production environment. Proper safeguards should be implemented when PT is conducted on the production environment.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.2.4
evidence.text: The frequency of PT should be determined based on factors such as system criticality and the system’s exposure to cyber risks. For systems that are directly accessible from the Internet, the FI is expected to conduct PT to validate the adequacy of the security controls at least once annually or whenever these systems undergo major changes or updates.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.3.1
evidence.text: The FI should carry out regular scenario-based cyber exercises to validate and review its response and recovery, as well as communication plans against cyber threats. These exercises could include social engineering, table-top, or cyber range exercises.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.3.2
evidence.text: Depending on the exercise objectives, the FI should involve relevant stakeholders, including senior management, business functions, corporate communications, crisis management team, service providers, and technical staff responsible for cyber threat detection, response and recovery.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.4.1
evidence.text: The FI is encouraged to perform an adversarial attack simulation exercise to test and validate the effectiveness of its cyber defence and response plan against prevalent cyber threats.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.4.2
evidence.text: The objectives, scope and rules of engagement should be defined before the commencement of the exercise, and the exercise should be conducted in a controlled manner under close supervision to ensure the activities carried out by the red team do not disrupt the FI’s production systems.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.5.1
evidence.text: To simulate realistic adversarial attacks on an FI during a red team exercise, the threat scenario should be designed and based on real cyber incidents.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.5.2
evidence.text: As an alternative, the FI could also design the exercise scenario by using threat intelligence that is relevant to their IT environment to identify threat actors who are most likely to pose a threat to the FI; and identify the tactics, techniques and procedures most likely to be used in such attacks.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 13.6.1
evidence.text: A comprehensive remediation management process should be established to track and resolve issues identified from the cyber security assessments or exercises. The process should minimally include the following: (a) severity assessment and classification of an issue; (b) timeframe to remediate issues of different severity; and (c) risk assessment and mitigation strategies to manage deviations from the framework.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.1
evidence.text: Application programming interfaces (APIs) enable various software applications to communicate and interact with each other and exchange data. Open APIs are publicly available APIs that provide developers with programmatic access to a proprietary software application or web service. FIs collaborate with FinTech companies and develop open APIs, which are used by third parties to implement products and services for customers and the marketplace. Hence, it is important for the FI to establish adequate safeguards to manage the development and provision of APIs for secure delivery of such services.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.2
evidence.text: To safeguard customer information and the integrity of its systems, the FI should implement strong controls to authorise and control access to designated API services.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.3
evidence.text: A well-defined vetting process should be implemented for assessing third parties’ suitability in connecting to the FI via APIs, as well as governing third party API access. The vetting criteria should take into account the third party’s nature of business, security policy, industry reputation and track record amongst others.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.4
evidence.text: The FI should perform risk assessment before allowing third parties to connect to its systems via APIs, and ensure the security implementation for each API is commensurate with the sensitivity and business criticality of the data being exchanged, and the confidentiality and integrity requirements of the data.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.5
evidence.text: Security standards for designing and developing secure APIs should be established. The standards should include the measures to protect the API keys or access tokens, which are used to authorise access to APIs to exchange confidential data. A reasonable timeframe should be defined and enforced for access token expiry to reduce the risk of unauthorised access.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.6
evidence.text: Strong encryption standards and key management controls should be adopted to secure transmission of sensitive data through APIs.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.7
evidence.text: A robust security screening and testing of the API should be performed between the FI and third party before it goes into production. The FI should have the ability to log the access sessions by the third party, such as the identity of the third party making the API connections, and the data being accessed.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.8
evidence.text: Real-time monitoring and alerting capabilities should be instituted to provide visibility of the usage and performance of APIs and detect suspicious activities. Robust measures should be established to promptly revoke the API keys or access token in the event of a breach.

evidence.title: TRM consultation draft (2019) · 6.4.9
evidence.text: The FI should implement measures to handle high volumes of API call requests by legitimate applications, and mitigate denial-of-service attacks. The measures to be implemented should be commensurate with the criticality and availability requirements of the application.

proposed_change_statements.summary: Access must now follow the roles of staff, contractors and service providers, and the principles apply to 'sensitive' rather than 'critical' functions.
The access process must also cover changes to access rights, and approval may come from appropriate parties such as the asset owner.
Multi-factor authentication now applies to 'sensitive' rather than 'critical' system functions, and protects 'data' rather than 'information'.
Reviews may be performed by appropriate parties, and must catch inappropriate access rather than only incorrectly provisioned access.
Remote devices must be 'secured' rather than 'hardened' according to the security standards, a broader requirement.
Minimum assessment scope now names open network ports and application vulnerabilities, and drops unapproved applications and services.
Exercises must 'validate' plans; the words 'and review' were removed, so the expected outcome changed slightly.
'Is encouraged to' became 'should': adversarial attack simulation moved from optional good practice to an expected practice.
Threat scenarios now apply to any cyber security assessment, not only red-team exercises, and use challenging but plausible threats rather than past incidents.
Threat intelligence is no longer 'an alternative' to incident-based scenarios but an additional design approach.
This draft paragraph is not kept as a separate paragraph in the final text; confirm whether other API controls cover it before retiring the mapping.
Vetting criteria now consider the third party's cyber security posture rather than its security policy.
Third-party API sessions must now be logged, including date and time, instead of the FI only having the ability to log them.
Real-time monitoring is now framed as detective measures such as real-time monitoring and alerting technologies.
The FI must ensure adequate system capacity and mitigate cyber threats such as DoS attacks; the proportionality wording was removed.
New in the final text: a policy and procedure must ensure third-party and open-source code is reviewed and tested before integration.
New in the final text: track updates and reported vulnerabilities for third-party and open-source code used in the FI's software.

scenario.title: Technology risk: from consultation draft to final rules
scenario.baseline_label: Prepared from the TRM consultation draft (March 2019)
scenario.context_note: The bank mapped the March 2019 consultation draft. MAS then issued the final Guidelines; only what changed needs fresh review.
scenario.legal_force_note: Both texts are MAS guidelines; legal force did not change.
suggested_questions: Which access control obligations changed in the final guidelines, and which controls should we review?
Why does the adversarial attack simulation obligation need review?
Where are the coverage gaps for the new open-source code obligations?
scenario.disclosure: Public MAS sources: verbatim paragraph excerpts from the March 2019 consultation draft and the January 2021 final Guidelines, chapters 6.4, 9 and 13 plus new paragraphs 6.1.3-6.1.4. Change classifications are team golden labels. Enterprise policies, controls and mappings are synthetic.
